c.entradas.dumuzi-tammuz.nombre_original: Dumu-zid (Sumerian, 'legitimate/faithful son'); Dumuzu or Duʾuzu (Akkadian); Tammuz (Hebrew and Aramaic)
c.entradas.dumuzi-tammuz.fecha_texto: Attested from the Early Dynastic period. His cult of lamentation survives into the 1st millennium BC and appears in Ezekiel 8:14.
c.entradas.dumuzi-tammuz.resumen: Shepherd god and husband of Inanna. After his wife leaves the Underworld, he must take her place there for half the year. He was the object of ritual laments.
c.entradas.dumuzi-tammuz.interpretacion:
Frazer made Dumuzi the model of the vegetation 'dying and rising god'. Current Assyriology heavily qualifies that idea: the texts dwell above all on his death and on mourning, and the alternation with his sister Geshtinanna is read in the context of the pastoral and agricultural cycle, not as a triumphant resurrection.

The Sumerian King List mentions two Dumuzis: an antediluvian king of Bad-tibira and a fisherman from Uruk. The courtship poems between Inanna and Dumuzi form an important body of love poetry.
c.entradas.dumuzi-tammuz.detalles.0: The fourth month of the Babylonian and Hebrew calendars, Du'uzu or Tammuz, bears his name.
c.entradas.dumuzi-tammuz.detalles.1: Ezekiel 8:14 describes women weeping for Tammuz at the gate of the temple in Jerusalem.
c.entradas.dumuzi-tammuz.detalles.2: 'Dumuzi's Dream' (ETCSL 1.4.3) tells of his pursuit by the galla demons.
c.entradas.dumuzi-tammuz.detalles.3: Together with Ningishzida, he is a doorkeeper of Anu's heaven in the myth of Adapa.
c.entradas.ninurta.nombre_original: Nin-urta (Sumerian, perhaps 'Lord of arable land', etymology debated); at Lagash, Nin-Ĝirsu
c.entradas.ninurta.fecha_texto: Attested from the Early Dynastic period as Ningirsu of Lagash. He was very important in Assyria in the 9th–8th centuries BC.
c.entradas.ninurta.resumen: Son of Enlil and a warrior and agricultural god. He is the champion of the gods against the monsters Anzu and Asag. He protected the fields and irrigation, but also the king's warfare.
c.entradas.ninurta.interpretacion:
Ninurta combines two functions that only seem opposed: the farmer and the warrior. Both defend civilized order against chaos, which comes from the mountains, the territory of enemies and monsters. At Lagash, Ningirsu had his great temple Eninnu, whose rebuilding is narrated in the Gudea Cylinders (c. 2125 BC).

In the 1st millennium BC, the Assyrian kings promoted him as a god of war and dedicated a temple to him at Kalhu (Nimrud). His fight against Anzu was a model for the exaltation of Marduk.
c.entradas.ninurta.detalles.0: His temple at Nippur is the Eshumesha; at Lagash, as Ningirsu, the Eninnu.
c.entradas.ninurta.detalles.1: His talking weapon is called Sharur.
c.entradas.ninurta.detalles.2: The Gudea Cylinders (Louvre) narrate the building of the Eninnu.
c.entradas.ninurta.detalles.3: Ashurnasirpal II built him a temple at Kalhu.
c.entradas.ninurta.fuentes_primarias.1: Lugal-e and Ninurta's Return to Nippur (ETCSL 1.6.1–1.6.2)
c.entradas.ninurta.fuentes_primarias.3: Reliefs from the temple of Ninurta at Nimrud
c.entradas.anunnaki.nombre_original: a-nun-na (Sumerian, 'offspring of An' or 'princely offspring'); Anunnakkū (Akkadian)
c.entradas.anunnaki.fecha_texto: The term is attested from the 3rd millennium BC. Its meaning changes over time, and it becomes more frequent from the Old Babylonian period onward.
c.entradas.anunnaki.resumen: Collective name for a group of gods, especially the great gods or the gods of highest rank. In later texts it comes to designate the gods of the Underworld. It is not the name of a race or a people.
c.entradas.anunnaki.interpretacion:
What the texts say: in Sumerian, the term is written a-nun-na or da-nun-na. It is usually understood as 'those of princely seed' or 'the offspring of An'. It contains no idea of 'coming from heaven to earth'. The translation 'those who from heaven to earth came', popularized by Zecharia Sitchin, does not correspond to the Sumerian language. In the Sumerian texts, the Anunna are the body of the principal gods, who form assemblies and decree destinies. Their number varies from text to text, and none attributes a planetary origin to them.

What the Akkadian texts say: in Atrahasis, the Anunnaki are the higher gods and the Igigi those who labor. From the Middle Babylonian period, the relationship is reversed or blurred: 'Anunnaki' designates the gods of the Underworld, for example Ereshkigal's judges, and 'Igigi' those of heaven. Black and Green stress that the usage is inconsistent and that the terms are sometimes used as synonyms. For Assyriology, the Anunnaki are a theological category within the pantheon, neither flesh-and-blood beings nor colonists from another planet.
c.entradas.anunnaki.detalles.0: Their name is written with the DINGIR sign (marker of divinity) plus a-nun-na.
c.entradas.anunnaki.detalles.1: In the Descent of Inanna, the seven Anunna, judges of the Underworld, condemn her with the look of death.
c.entradas.anunnaki.detalles.2: In the Enuma Elish, Marduk divides the Anunnaki into 300 of heaven and 300 of the Underworld, and they build Babylon and the Esagila.
c.entradas.anunnaki.detalles.3: In Atrahasis, the Anunnaki rule and the Igigi labor until they rebel.
c.entradas.anunnaki.detalles.4: No cuneiform text connects the Anunnaki with Nibiru or with gold mining.
c.entradas.igigi.fecha_texto: Attested mainly from the Old Babylonian period.
c.entradas.igigi.resumen: Collective name for a group of gods in Akkadian texts. In Atrahasis they are the lesser gods forced to labor, who rebel. In later texts they are the gods of heaven, as opposed to the Anunnaki of the Underworld.
c.entradas.igigi.interpretacion:
The word has no clear etymology and is not Sumerian in origin. In Atrahasis, the rebellion of the Igigi, who burn their tools and surround Enlil's house, serves to explain the origin of human labor: humans are created to do that work.

The term seems to change meaning depending on the period, as happens with 'Anunnaki'. Some sources count 300 Igigi in heaven, but the figures vary from text to text. It is a theological category, not a historical group.
c.entradas.igigi.detalles.0: In Atrahasis they dig the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.
c.entradas.igigi.detalles.1: Their rebellion takes place at night before Enlil's temple, the Ekur.
c.entradas.igigi.detalles.2: In texts of the 1st millennium BC the formula 'the Igigi and the Anunnaki' is used to refer to all the gods.
c.entradas.me.fecha_texto: The concept is attested in Sumerian literature of the 3rd millennium BC and the Old Babylonian period.
c.entradas.me.resumen: The me are the principles, powers and norms that make civilization and worship possible: kingship, priesthood, the crafts, the arts, justice and many more. The gods possess them, guard them and can hand them over.
c.entradas.me.interpretacion:
Kramer and Jacobsen understood them as 'divine norms' or 'decrees' of cultural order. What is distinctive is that they are conceived as something concrete: Inanna can load them onto a boat. That is why some scholars describe them as 'essences' or 'properties' that take material form in insignia and rituals.

The list in 'Inanna and Enki' is the main source on the content of the me and mixes institutions, activities, emotions and objects. There is nothing of technology or artifacts about them; they are the Sumerian way of expressing that the social order has a divine origin.
c.entradas.me.detalles.0: 'Inanna and Enki' lists more than a hundred me.
c.entradas.me.detalles.1: They include kingship and priesthood as well as deceit, sexuality, music, carpentry and the destruction of cities.
c.entradas.me.detalles.2: One of Inanna's epithets is 'lady of all the me' (nin-me-šar2-ra).
c.entradas.me.detalles.3: In Akkadian they are rendered as paršū, 'rites, ordinances'.
c.entradas.apkallu-oannes.nombre_origina: abgal (Sumerian) / apkallu (Akkadian), 'sage'; Oannes, Greek form of Uanna (U-An) in Berossus
c.entradas.apkallu-oannes.fecha_texto: The tradition of the sages is attested from the 2nd millennium BC. The iconography is mainly Neo-Assyrian (9th–7th centuries BC). The Uruk List of Kings and Sages dates to 165 BC, and Berossus wrote c. 290–280 BC.
c.entradas.apkallu-oannes.resumen: The apkallu are seven primordial sages whom, according to Babylonian tradition, Ea sent before the flood to teach humans the arts of civilization. The first was Uanna, the Oannes of Berossus, who came out of the sea in the form of a fish-man. In Assyrian art they appear as protective figures.
c.entradas.apkallu-oannes.interpretacion:
What the texts say: the Uruk List of Kings and Sages (165 BC) pairs each of the seven antediluvian kings with an apkallu, beginning with Uanna alongside Ayalu of Eridu, and continues with post-flood sages, by then human (ummānu). In the ritual series bīt mēseri and in incantation texts, the apkallu appear as creatures of Ea, 'pure carp of the Apsu', and protect against demons. Berossus, a Babylonian priest who wrote in Greek, relates that Oannes came out of the Erythraean Sea (the Gulf) and taught writing, the sciences, the arts, the founding of cities and temples, and agriculture. His work has been lost and we know it from quotations by later authors. Oannes was once thought to be another name for Ea, but today he is considered the Greek form of Uanna.

Iconography: Neo-Assyrian reliefs, for example from the palace of Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud, show three types of apkallu. One has a bird's head and wings, another a human form with wings, and another wears a fish skin or 'cloak' over the head and back. They usually carry a cone (mullilu, 'purifier') and a bucket (banduddû). They are understood to be performing a ritual of purification and protection for the king or the palace. Ritual texts indicate that exorcist priests dressed in fish cloaks to represent the sages. According to Assyriologists, they are apotropaic protective spirits. The 'bucket' is a ritual vessel, not a handbag or a device, and the 'fish cloak' is a symbolic attribute of their link with Ea's Apsu.
c.entradas.apkallu-oannes.detalles.0: The Uruk List of Kings and Sages (W 20030,7) was found in the Bit Resh at Uruk in 1959–1960 and is dated to 165 BC.
c.entradas.apkallu-oannes.detalles.1: Uanna-Adapa is the first sage in several traditions; Adapa is also 'the sage of Eridu'.
c.entradas.apkallu-oannes.detalles.2: In incantations, apkallu figurines are placed beneath the floors of houses to protect them.
c.entradas.apkallu-oannes.detalles.3: The Nimrud reliefs show them with a purification cone (mullilu) and a vessel (banduddû).
c.entradas.apkallu-oannes.detalles.4: Berossus dedicated his Babyloniaká to Antiochus I, c. 290–280 BC.
